title: Rethinking Uncertainty Estimation in LLMs: A Principled Single-Sequence Measure
claim: Greedy and beam search are biased estimators of entropy but near-exact estimators of the maximum sequence likelihood, unlike sampling.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, shaded variance bands, starred greedy point
description: Two side-by-side line charts share the x-axis, 'Number of samples / Beam width', running from 1 to 20. Panel (a), 'Estimating H(p(y))', plots the estimation error of entropy. Beam search, in blue, sits well above zero, between about 2 and 1.2, with a narrow band. Multinomial sampling at temperatures 1 and 0.7, in green and orange, hug zero with wide pink-orange bands that shrink as samples increase. Panel (b), 'Estimating M(p(y))', plots error of the maximum sequence log-likelihood. Beam search and greedy decoding, a blue star at x=1, sit at zero with almost no spread. Sampling curves start far below zero, down to about -6, and slowly converge. A legend sits at lower right of (b). The eye goes first to the blue line and star.
caption: Quality of estimators for synthetic predictive distributions $p(\By)$ with $|\cV|=20$ and $T=4$. The predictive entropy $\ENT ( p(\By) )$ is estimated as in Eq. [ref] using multinomial sampling (MS) with different temperatures ($\tau$). The negative maximum sequence log-likelihood $\rM(p(\By))$ is estimated by the maximum over $N$ samples obtained by beam search ($N=1$ represents greedy decoding) or MS with different $\tau$. Statistics are obtained by sampling 2000 different $p(\By)$. (a) Lines show average, shades denote one std. (b) Lines show the median, and shades denote the 5% to 95% quantile range.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly employed in real-world applications, driving the need to evaluate the trustworthiness of their generated text. To this end, reliable uncertainty estimation is essential. Leading uncertainty estimation methods generate and analyze multiple output sequences, which is computationally expensive and impractical at scale. In this work, we inspect the theoretical foundations of these methods and explore new directions to enhance computational efficiency. Building on the framework of proper scoring rules, we find that the negative log-likelihood of the most likely output sequence constitutes a theoretically principled uncertainty measure. To approximate this alternative measure, we propose G-NLL, obtained using a single output sequence from greedy decoding. This approach streamlines uncertainty estimation while preserving theoretical rigor. Empirical results demonstrate that G-NLL achieves state-of-the-art performance across various scenarios. Our work lays the theoretical foundation for efficient and reliable uncertainty estimation in natural language generation, challenging the necessity of the prevalent methods that are more complex and resource-intensive.
